overview: Chasmosaurus belli was a chasmosaurine ceratopsid from the Campanian of Alberta (~76 Ma), notable for its enormous frill relative to body size — larger proportionally than any other ceratopsid. The frill contained two large parietal fenestrae (openings) that reduced its weight while maintaining its impressive visual size, and a network of blood vessels supplied the skin covering the frill, enabling colour flushing for display.

Chasmosaurus is the namesake of Chasmosaurinae — the chasmosaurine lineage that ultimately produced Triceratops. Unlike the relatively short frills of centrosaurines, chasmosaurines evolved increasingly large, elongated frills. Chasmosaurus itself shows variation in skull and frill morphology between specimens, some of which may reflect sexual dimorphism.

fossilSites.note: Campanian coastal plain deposits with multiple Chasmosaurus specimens including the type and beautifully preserved skulls.

fossilSites.name: Aguja Formation
fossilSites.note: Campanian deposits with Chasmosaurus-like material extending the known range southward.

articles.title: Discovery and the chasmosaurine lineage
articles.body: Named by Lambe in 1914 from Dinosaur Park Formation material; Lambe's Monoclonius belli was later reassigned to Chasmosaurus. The genus is pivotal for understanding chasmosaurine evolution: it shows the large frill and relatively modest nasal horn that characterise early chasmosaurines, before the later evolution of elaborate brow horns and larger nasal horns in Triceratops-grade animals.

articles.title: Frill biology
articles.body: The chasmosaurine frill is structurally different from the centrosaurine frill: larger, with bigger parietal fenestrae covered by a thin skin membrane in life. Vascular channels in the frill bones indicate blood flow that could flush the skin with colour. The enormous display surface was almost certainly brightly patterned in life, used for species recognition, mate choice and possibly threat displays.

articles.title: Sexual dimorphism
articles.body: Two frill morphs are present in Chasmosaurus specimens from the same formation: one with a squamosal notch and oval frill (the B morph) and one without (the A morph). These may represent male and female, with the more elaborate frill being male. Similar sexual dimorphism has been proposed for other ceratopsids.

fossilRecord.material: Skulls, skeletons and bonebeds; multiple species recognised.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Cretaceous coastal plain of Alberta alongside Corythosaurus, Parasaurolophus and Gorgosaurus.
fossilRecord.evidence: Multiple skulls with different frill shapes document intraspecific or interspecific variation in the chasmosaurine lineage.

record.description: Chasmosaurus was a long-frilled chasmosaurine ceratopsid from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta. Numerous skulls and skeletons, including juveniles and skin impressions, document its anatomy, while species limits and the significance of frill variation remain debated.
facts: C. belli is securely recognised; C. russelli is also commonly retained, whereas Vagaceratops is generally separate.
Large frill openings and marginal ornaments are preserved, but display, species recognition and sexual selection are hypotheses.

review.ageReviewNote: Diagnostic Chasmosaurus material is late Campanian in the Dinosaur Park Formation.

evidence.material: Numerous skulls and partial to nearly complete skeletons across growth stages, with some skin impressions.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Anatomy and growth are strong; species diagnoses, colour and social-display functions remain uncertain.
